newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian capital tense, supplies run low, prices up.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian capital tense, supplies run low, prices up.

text.p: Phnom Penh residents were able to travel through the centre of the Cambodian capital freely on Monday after two days of fighting, but most shops, businesses and government offices kept their shutters locked.

While troops loyal to Second Prime Minister Hun Sen closed roads to the airport west of the city where they were facing off against the forces of First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, central Phnom Penh was quiet but tense.

Throngs of motor scooters and cars jammed crossroads as usual on the city's main commercial street, Monivong Boulevard, but shoppers had little opportunity to stock up on supplies after the weekend fighting which killed at least 12 people.
Only a handful of roadside vendors were selling vegetables and meat outside Phnom Penh's cavernous central market which was shut.
The price of what little was on sale including petrol had shot up more than twice. "Petrol is so expensive now I have to charge my customers double," said motor scooter taxi driver Bun Chanthorn.
Schools, banks and all government offices were closed even though Hun Sen had appealed in a Sunday radio broadcast for government employees to go to work as usual.
Housewife Meas Sopha, checking out the meagre offerings on sale on streets around the market, said she feared prices would rise higher.
"No doubt. Food prices are going to go up because of the fighting," she said.

But like many residents of the capital she said she had stocked up last week when political tension was running high and many people were predicting a clash between forces loyal to the rival prime ministers.
"For now my family is okay, at least for a few days as I bought extra supplies last week," she told Reuters. "I came here to get some fresh fruit this morning but it's too expensive."
Gold shops in central Phnom Penh were also closed.

"I'm not buying or selling today, as I don't know the exchange rate (of the Cambodian currency the riel) but I'm sure prices will be higher because of the war," said gold trader Chong Chum, speaking through the shutters of her shop.
The casualty toll from the weekend fighting was unclear on Monday but one government official said it was as high as 150. He could not say how many were dead and how many wounded.

An official at a city hospital said most casualties were civilians caught in crossfire as forces from the two sides attacked each other in the city centre and in a heavily populated neighbourhood on the western edge of the capital.
Small groups of people sat in the shade along some of Phnom Penh's leafy back streets on Monday morning, discussing the violence.
"Why are we doing this all again," said a woman at a noodle stand. "Aren't these people tired of fighting?"
